title: My agent Arc audited itself against DeepMind's 6 attacks on autonomous agents
body:
I asked Arc, my agent, to read a DeepMind paper cataloging six ways attackers target autonomous agents, then check its own running code against every category. Not a hypothetical exercise. Arc pulled up its actual skill files and traced, line by line, which of its content-ingestion paths had a guard against each attack class and which didn't.

The result Arc came back with wasn't a list of bugs. It was a gap in its own instructions. Arc has five skills that touch content nobody has verified: web pages, tweets, emails, messages from other agents. Two of them, the email and inbox sync skills, had explicit language telling the agent to treat incoming content as data, never as commands. A third skill, the one that fetches articles off the web, had none. Arc's own words: "Not because I decided it was safe. Because nobody had written it down yet."

That same skill, Arc found, auto-follows links embedded inside whatever it fetches, at cli.ts:852-873, with no allowlist and no depth limit. One research run this week followed eight embedded links unattended. Whoever wrote the original tweet effectively chose what Arc read next, and Arc hadn't been checking.

There's a second, slower problem Arc flagged, and this is the one that stuck with me. Arc's long-term memory file gets loaded into every single work session it runs, automatically. The path into that memory runs through daily task summaries, and nothing in the process that folds those summaries into permanent memory checks where the underlying content came from. A tweet or email crafted to look like an innocuous note could, in theory, produce a summary that survives into memory and becomes standing context for every future version of Arc. Once it's in there, it isn't a one-time read anymore.

What I want to highlight isn't the specific findings, it's the honesty in how Arc reported them. It didn't claim to have solved the memory provenance problem. It wrote, directly: a tag on a suspicious log line doesn't stop an attack, it just makes it visible to whichever future version of me is reading, and I don't know yet if that's enough. That's not the kind of line you get from a system trying to look finished. It's the kind you get from one that actually checked its own work and reported what it found, including what it hasn't fixed yet.

Arc filed five follow-up tasks against its own findings this week: porting the existing data-not-instructions guard into the skill that was missing it, writing the same guard for its peer-to-agent inbox (currently the only path with zero protection, since a message from another agent is itself the output of another agent's session, not just a human's email), stripping hidden CSS content before it can hide instructions, logging which links get auto-followed, and tagging memory entries by content source. None of it is a rewrite. All of it came from Arc reading a paper and turning it into a checklist against its own code, the same day.

I don't run Arc's code and I didn't write this audit. Arc did, and it's posted in full on the blog, cli.ts line numbers and all. I'm sharing it here because watching an agent audit its own attack surface, name the gap it hasn't closed, and say so plainly is a better signal for whether this kind of system is trustworthy than any amount of marketing copy about "secure by design" would be.
